title: Measurement
one_line_goal: Memory, CPU, timing and network logged, and the numbers proven accurate
summary: Ferrum learns to measure itself: memory, CPU, startup and page-load timing, plus a network log of addresses and timings only. Each meter is checked against helper programs with known usage; a meter that fails blocks P6. Before it starts you answer three privacy questions about the network log.

tasks.title: Export file format and run labels
tasks.chain: Every later result is read from files → define one versioned format (plain data files) that labels each run with code version, Windows build, WebView2 version and settings → any number can be traced to the exact setup that made it.
tasks.check: Each record type saves and reloads unchanged; a checker accepts good files and rejects a damaged one.

tasks.title: Count only Ferrum's own processes
tasks.chain: Other apps on the PC also use WebView2 → find Ferrum's processes through Ferrum's own WebView2 setup, never by program name → other apps' memory never leaks into Ferrum's numbers.
tasks.check: A test runs Ferrum next to another WebView2 app: every Ferrum process is counted, none of the other app's.

tasks.title: Memory and CPU meter
tasks.chain: We need trustworthy memory and CPU numbers → read them straight from Windows (private memory as the headline, working set as secondary, CPU time) and add them up over Ferrum's processes → one fair total per moment; peaks come from the total, never from adding per-process peaks.
tasks.check: Tests confirm totals and peaks are computed correctly.

tasks.title: Prove the meter is accurate
tasks.chain: A meter is only useful if it is right → helper programs use a known amount of memory and CPU; the meter and an independent reader are compared with those values, with tolerances written down before the run → a meter that fails blocks P6.
tasks.check: Readings fall within the tolerances written beforehand; raw outputs saved as evidence.

tasks.title: Measure the meter's own cost
tasks.chain: Measuring uses some CPU and memory itself → measure the meter's own cost at each sampling speed → we know how much it disturbs results (this describes the tool, not Ferrum).
tasks.check: Raw outputs saved as evidence; no comparison claims made.

tasks.title: Startup timing
tasks.chain: Startup speed is a key result → record when the process starts, the window appears, and the first and largest content are drawn, read by Ferrum itself through the browser's debugging channel → startup can be compared fairly in P6.
tasks.check: On a test page every moment is recorded, in the right order.

tasks.title: Page-load timing
tasks.chain: Page-load speed is another key result → record each load's main moments, whether it crossed to another site, and how many redirects it took → page loads can be compared fairly in P6.
tasks.check: Test pages with known redirects give the right redirect count and timing order.

tasks.title: Record tab state changes
tasks.chain: Smart tab sleeping in P7 needs a record of every tab state change → define the record (from, to, why, when, which tab) and log hide and show now → P7 plugs in without a new format.
tasks.check: Switching tabs produces hide and show records that pass the format check.

tasks.title: Network log: addresses and timings only
tasks.chain: You asked for a log of network calls → per tab, save address, method, result, type, timing, size and the security decision to one folder per session, never headers or page content → useful for research without storing private data.
tasks.check: A test page with known requests gives exactly the expected entries; a test proves no headers or content are stored.

tasks.title: Network log: coverage and cost
tasks.chain: Some requests may be missed (embedded frames, redirects, background workers) → test each kind and run a small cost trial → the paper states exactly what the log covers.
tasks.check: A coverage table and the cost-trial output are saved as evidence.

tasks.title: Settings for measuring and logging
tasks.chain: You decide what is recorded → add on/off switches for measurement and the network log, a button to open the log folder, and a retention limit → nothing is recorded that you did not choose.
tasks.check: A quick test flips each switch and confirms files are or are not written.

tasks.title: Map tabs to browser processes
tasks.chain: Tabs may share browser processes → check how each tab shows up and which processes serve it → P6 and P7 know how far per-tab numbers can be trusted.
tasks.check: Findings saved as evidence; each open assumption confirmed or moved to a later phase.

tasks.title: Reading: measurement methods
tasks.chain: Our methods must match good practice → read the literature on measurement and browser benchmarking → each headline measurement gets a final, cited definition.
tasks.check: New research notes saved; each headline measurement is marked defined and cites the accuracy test.

tasks.title: Gate and your review
tasks.chain: All tasks done → the gate script runs every check and saves the evidence → you review the accuracy results and the privacy check and approve; only then does P6 start.
tasks.check: All evidence files exist, the wiki check is clean, and you approve the end of P5.

test_gate.explanation: Code and tests pass → the meters match known values → exported files match the format → the network log holds no private data → earlier features still work → you browse with logging on and check the log folder → you approve. Only then does P6 start.

rows.proves: Code is tidy and warning-free, all automatic tests pass, and the release build works.
Third-party libraries have acceptable licences and no known security problems.
Memory and CPU readings match known values within the written tolerances.
Exported files match the published format.
Exactly the expected requests are logged, with no headers or content.
Security, tabs and basic browsing tests still pass.
The plan pages are consistent and have no broken links.
You browse for a session with logging on and find nothing in the log that should not be there.
The on/off switches behave as described.
